\section{Searching}

\entry{Binary search on the answer}{$O(\log)$}{%
No template needed. The predicate must be monotone false$\dots$false
true$\dots$true; keep the invariant \code{pred(lo)} false, \code{pred(hi)} true and
loop \code{while (hi - lo > 1)} with \code{m = lo + (hi-lo)/2}; the answer is
\code{hi}. On a sorted array use \code{lower\_bound}/\code{upper\_bound}, or
\code{partition\_point(all(v), pred)}.\\[0.3ex]
Almost every ``minimise the maximum'' / ``can we do it within $k$'' problem is this
plus a greedy check. Reals: fix the iteration count (100 halvings) instead of looping
on a tolerance, which can spin forever.}

\entry{Ternary search}{$O(\log(b-a))$}{%
From KACTL. \code{ternSearch(a, b, f)}: the smallest \code{i} in \code{[a, b]} that
\textbf{maximises} \code{f(i)}, assuming $f(a) < \dots < f(i) \ge \dots \ge f(b)$. To
\textbf{minimise}, change the \code{<} at (A) and at (B) to \code{>}. To allow flat
stretches on the other side, make (A) \code{<=} and reverse the loop at
(B).\\[0.3ex]
Usage: \code{int ind = ternSearch(0, n-1, [\&](int i)\{ return a[i]; \});}. Reals:
the classic thirds loop, 200 iterations, on \code{ld}.}

%LABEL ternSearch
\begin{lstlisting}
template<class F>
int ternSearch(int a, int b, F f) {
    assert(a <= b);
    while (b - a >= 5) {
        int mid = (a + b) / 2;
        if (f(mid) < f(mid+1)) a = mid; // (A)
        else b = mid+1;
    }
    rep(i,a+1,b+1) if (f(a) < f(i)) a = i; // (B)
    return a;
}
\end{lstlisting}

\entry{Coordinate compression}{$O(n \log n)$}{%
Maps arbitrary values onto \code{0 .. k-1} keeping order, so a \code{BIT} or \code{Seg}
can index them. This is what lets you avoid \code{SparseSeg} whenever the whole input is
readable up front --- which is almost always.\\[0.3ex]
Remember to compress \emph{every} value you will ever look up, queries included, not
just the ones in the array. For half-open interval problems add both \code{l} and
\code{r} (and sometimes \code{r+1}).}

\begin{lstlisting}
// returns the sorted distinct values; id(v) is v's index
vi compress(vi vals) {
    sort(all(vals));
    vals.erase(unique(all(vals)), vals.end());
    return vals;
}
int id(const vi& c, ll v) {
    return (int)(lower_bound(all(c), v) - c.begin());
}
\end{lstlisting}

\entry{Interval cover}{$O(n \log n)$}{%
Fewest intervals from \code{I} that together cover the target \code{G}; returns their
indices, or empty if impossible. Intervals are \textbf{half-open} \code{[a, b)}; for
closed ones on integers use \code{[a, b+1)}. Greedy: from the current point, among the
intervals starting at or before it, take the one that reaches furthest. Same idea for
``fewest jumps'' and ``fewest refuelling stops'' problems. From KACTL.}

%LABEL cover
\begin{lstlisting}
template<class T>
vector<int> cover(pair<T,T> G, vector<pair<T,T>> I) {
    vector<int> S(I.size()), R;
    iota(all(S), 0);
    sort(all(S), [&](int a, int b) { return I[a] < I[b]; });
    T cur = G.first;
    int at = 0;
    while (cur < G.second) {
        pair<T, int> mx = make_pair(cur, -1);
        while (at < (int)I.size() && I[S[at]].first <= cur) {
            mx = max(mx, make_pair(I[S[at]].second, S[at]));
            at++;
        }
        if (mx.second == -1) return {};
        cur = mx.first;
        R.push_back(mx.second);
    }
    return R;
}
\end{lstlisting}

\section{Reference}

\entry{What fits in the time limit}{$\sim10^8$ simple ops/s at \code{-O2}}{%
{\ttfamily\footnotesize
\begin{ctab}{0.20}{0.75}
n <= 10 & O(n!) \hfill brute force permutations\\
n <= 20 & O(2\^{}n n) \hfill bitmask DP, PathDP\\
n <= 40 & O(2\^{}(n/2)) \hfill meet in the middle\\
n <= 100 & O(n\^{}4) \hfill 4 nested loops, Hungarian\\
n <= 500 & O(n\^{}3) \hfill Floyd, matrix, interval DP\\
n <= 5000 & O(n\^{}2) \hfill pairwise DP\\
n <= 1e5 & O(n log\^{}2 n) \hfill HLD + Seg\\
n <= 1e6 & O(n log n) \hfill sort, Seg, Dijkstra\\
n <= 1e7 & O(n) \hfill sieve, two pointers\\
n <= 1e18 & O(log n) \hfill binary search, matrix power\\
\end{ctab}}\\[0.3ex]
A \code{map} / \code{set} operation costs $\sim$10x a \code{vector} one; sorting
$10^6$ \code{ll} is $\sim$0.1 s; $10^8$ additions is $\sim$0.1 s but $10^8$ random
memory accesses is $\sim$1 s. If $n \le 18$ and nothing else fits, it is a bitmask.}

\entry{Overflow and precision}{read this when a big test fails}{%
\code{ll} holds $9.2\cdot10^{18}$, \code{int} only $2.1\cdot10^9$ --- and
\code{n*(n-1)/2} already overflows \code{int} at \code{n = 1e5}.\\[0.3ex]
Use \code{INF = 1e18}, never \code{LLONG\_MAX}: \code{INF + INF} still fits, so a
forgotten guard gives a wrong answer instead of undefined behaviour. Guard anyway.\\[0.3ex]
\code{a * b \% m} overflows once $m > 3\cdot10^9$ --- cast to \code{i128}.
\code{cross} on coordinates up to $10^9$ reaches $2\cdot10^{18}$: fine, barely.\\[0.3ex]
\code{-7 \% 3 == -1} in C++. Normalise with \code{((x \% m) + m) \% m}.\\[0.3ex]
\code{pow(10, 2)} can return \code{99.999...}; never use \code{pow} for integers.
\code{sqrt(x)} likewise --- take \code{(ll)sqrtl(x)} then fix up by $\pm1$ in a loop.\\[0.3ex]
Compare squared distances, never \code{sqrt}ed ones. \code{double} has 15--16 significant
digits, \code{long double} 18--19 on x86.}

\entry{Pitfalls}{the usual wrong answers}{%
\textbf{Multiple test cases:} clear every global, resize every vector, reset
\code{cnt}/\code{timer}. The most common repeat-offender bug there is.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Recursion depth:} a DFS on a path of $2\cdot10^5$ vertices can blow the stack.
The iterative \code{euler}, \code{SCC}, \code{Bridges}, \code{centroids},
\code{eulerPath}, \code{Dinic}, \code{MCMF}, \code{Matching} and
\code{centroidTree} here are safe; \code{HLD} is not.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Output:} \code{'\textbackslash n'} not \code{endl} (\code{endl} flushes).
Keep \code{sync\_with\_stdio(false)}, and then never mix \code{printf} with
\code{cout}.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{\code{unordered\_map}} is $O(n)$ per operation against a crafted test; use
\code{map}, or add a random offset to every key.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Comparators} must be a strict weak ordering --- \code{<=} in a \code{sort}
comparator is a crash, not a wrong answer.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{\code{vector<bool>}} is a proxy type; \code{auto\& x = v[i]} does not do what you
expect. \textbf{Iterators} invalidate on \code{push\_back}.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Reading:} after \code{cin >> n}, a following \code{getline} reads the rest of that
line. Interactive problems need an explicit flush.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Edge cases:} $n = 1$, $n = 0$, an empty string, all elements equal, a
disconnected graph, self-loops, multi-edges, duplicate points, collinear points.}

\entry{Combinatorics}{}{%
$\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n-1}{k-1} + \binom{n-1}{k}$; hockey stick
$\sum_{i=r}^{n}\binom{i}{r} = \binom{n+1}{r+1}$; Vandermonde
$\sum_k \binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{p-k} = \binom{m+n}{p}$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Stars and bars.} $n$ identical items into $k$ ordered boxes:
$\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$, and $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ if every box must be non-empty.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Catalan} $C_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$: balanced bracket strings,
binary trees on $n$ nodes, triangulations of an $(n{+}2)$-gon, paths under the
diagonal. $1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Derangements} $D_n = (n-1)(D_{n-1} + D_{n-2})$, $D_0 = 1$, $D_1 = 0$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Inclusion-exclusion}
$|\bigcup A_i| = \sum|A_i| - \sum|A_i \cap A_j| + \dots$ --- over $\le 20$ sets this is
a mask loop with $(-1)^{\mathrm{popcount}}$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Burnside.} Orbits = average number of fixed points over the group. Necklaces of
$n$ beads in $k$ colours under rotation: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} k^{\gcd(i,n)}$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Lucas.} $\binom{n}{k} \bmod p$ for prime $p$ = product of
$\binom{n_i}{k_i}$ over the base-$p$ digits (0 if any $k_i > n_i$).\\[0.3ex]
$\sum_{i\le n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$, $\sum i^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$,
$\sum i^3 = \left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$.}

\entry{Number theory}{}{%
$\gcd(a,b)\cdot\mathrm{lcm}(a,b) = ab$ --- compute \code{a / gcd * b} to avoid
overflow.\\[0.3ex]
$\varphi(n) = n\prod_{p\mid n}(1-\frac1p)$; $\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d) = n$.
Fermat: $a^{p-1} \equiv 1$ for prime $p \nmid a$. Euler:
$a^{\varphi(m)} \equiv 1$ when $\gcd(a,m)=1$.\\[0.3ex]
$d(n) = \prod(e_i+1)$ divisors, $\sigma(n) = \prod\frac{p_i^{e_i+1}-1}{p_i-1}$.
The number of divisors stays small: at most 240 below $10^9$, 1344 below
$10^{18}$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Legendre.} The exponent of $p$ in $n!$ is
$\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor n/p^i \rfloor$ --- that is how you count trailing zeros of a
factorial.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{M\"obius} $\mu(n)$ is $0$ with a squared factor, else $(-1)^{\#\text{primes}}$;
$\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d) = [n=1]$, which turns ``count coprime pairs'' into a divisor
sum.\\[0.3ex]
Primes below $10^k$: $4$, $25$, $168$, $1229$, $9592$, $78498$, $664579$, $5761455$.
The gap between consecutive primes near $10^{18}$ stays under 1500.}

\entry{Graph facts}{}{%
\textbf{Max flow = min cut.} \textbf{K\"onig} (bipartite): max matching = min vertex
cover, and max independent set $= n - $ max matching. \textbf{Hall:} a perfect matching
on the left exists iff every subset $S$ of the left has
$|N(S)| \ge |S|$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Dilworth:} the minimum number of chains covering a poset equals the largest
antichain --- in practice a bipartite matching or an LIS.\\[0.3ex]
Bipartite iff no odd cycle. A tree has $n-1$ edges and a unique path between any two
vertices. A connected graph has an Euler circuit iff every degree is even (directed: in
= out everywhere).\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Planar:} $V - E + F = 2$, so $E \le 3V - 6$ and some vertex has degree
$\le 5$. Four colours always suffice, five are easy to find.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Spanning trees:} Cayley gives $n^{n-2}$ labelled trees on $n$ vertices; for a
general graph it is any cofactor of the Laplacian (Matrix-Tree), i.e. one
determinant (Gauss mod $p$: product of the pivots, sign flips per row swap).\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Pick:} a lattice polygon has $A = I + B/2 - 1$, with
$B = \sum \gcd(|dx|,|dy|)$ over the edges.}

\entry{Games (Sprague-Grundy)}{}{%
Two players alternate, the one who cannot move loses, both play perfectly, nothing is
hidden and there is no luck. Every position gets a number, its \textbf{Grundy value}:
$g(x) = \mathrm{mex}\{g(y) : y \text{ reachable from } x\}$, where mex is the smallest
non-negative integer \emph{not} in the set. A position with no moves has $g = 0$. The
player to move \textbf{loses iff $g = 0$}.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Several independent games at once} (move in exactly one of them per turn): the
Grundy value of the whole thing is the \textbf{XOR} of the parts. Nim: piles of sizes
$a_i$, take any amount from one pile; $g = a_1 \oplus a_2 \oplus \dots$. A move that
splits one game into two gives the XOR of the two halves as one option.\\[0.3ex]
In practice: compute $g$ for small sizes by brute force with memo, print them, look for
the pattern (periodic, $n \bmod k$, \dots), then prove or trust it. Mis\`ere Nim (last
to move loses): same as Nim unless every pile is $\le 1$; then the player to move wins
iff the number of piles is even.
Staircase Nim: only piles on odd steps matter. ``Take $1..k$ from one pile'':
$g = a \bmod (k+1)$.}

\entry{More counting}{}{%
\textbf{Stirling 2nd kind} $S(n,k)$: ways to split $n$ labelled items into $k$
non-empty unlabelled groups. $S(n,k) = k\,S(n{-}1,k) + S(n{-}1,k{-}1)$. Onto functions
$n \to k$: $k!\,S(n,k)$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Bell} $B_n = \sum_k S(n,k)$: all ways to split $n$ items into groups.
$1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203, 877, 4140$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Stirling 1st kind} $c(n,k)$: permutations of $n$ with exactly $k$ cycles.
$c(n,k) = (n{-}1)\,c(n{-}1,k) + c(n{-}1,k{-}1)$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Partitions} $p(n)$ of $n$ into a sum of positive integers (order does not
matter): dp \code{p[0] = 1; for each part k: for i >= k: p[i] += p[i-k]}. $p(100) \approx
1.9\cdot10^8$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Multinomial} $\binom{n}{k_1, \dots, k_m} = \frac{n!}{k_1! \cdots k_m!}$:
arrangements of a word with repeated letters.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Expected value} is linear even for dependent events: expected number of X =
sum over all candidates of P(candidate is X). Expected tries until a success of
probability $p$: $1/p$. Collect all $n$ coupons: $n H_n \approx n \ln n$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Grid paths} from $(0,0)$ to $(a,b)$: $\binom{a+b}{a}$. Those that never touch
the line $y = x + 1$ ($a \ge b$, reflection trick): $\binom{a+b}{a} - \binom{a+b}{a+1}$.}

\entry{Geometry formulas}{}{%
Triangle with sides $a, b, c$, $s = (a+b+c)/2$: area
$\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$ (Heron); $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos\gamma$;
$\frac{a}{\sin\alpha} = 2R$; circumradius $R = \frac{abc}{4A}$; inradius $r = A / s$.\\[0.3ex]
Angle between vectors $u, v$: \code{atan2(cross, dot)} --- signed and stable, better than
\code{acos}. Distance from point $p$ to line $ab$: $|(b-a)\times(p-a)| / |b-a|$.\\[0.3ex]
Circle sector area $\frac12 r^2\theta$, segment area $\frac12 r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)$,
chord length $2r\sin(\theta/2)$.\\[0.3ex]
Sphere: $V = \frac43\pi r^3$, $A = 4\pi r^2$; cap of height $h$: $V = \frac{\pi h^2
(3r - h)}{3}$, $A = 2\pi r h$. Cone / pyramid: $V = \frac13 \cdot$ base $\cdot$ height.\\[0.3ex]
Great-circle distance, latitude $\varphi$, longitude $\lambda$:
$d = r \arccos(\sin\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2 + \cos\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2\cos\Delta\lambda)$.\\[0.3ex]
Polygon on lattice points: Pick, see \emph{Graph facts}. Volume of a polyhedron with
outward faces: $\frac16\sum_{\text{faces}} (a \times b)\cdot c$ over triangulated
faces.}

\entry{Vectors and linear algebra}{}{%
\textbf{Cross product.} 2D: $a \times b = a_x b_y - a_y b_x$ $= |a||b|\sin\theta$; $> 0$
iff $b$ is counter-clockwise from $a$. Triangle area $= \frac12|(b-a)\times(c-a)|$.
3D: $a \times b = (a_y b_z - a_z b_y,\; a_z b_x - a_x b_z,\; a_x b_y - a_y b_x)$,
perpendicular to both, length = parallelogram area. $a\cdot(b\times c)$ = signed volume
of the parallelepiped (tetrahedron: $\frac16$); $=0$ iff coplanar.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Dot} $a\cdot b = |a||b|\cos\theta$; projection of $p$ on $u$:
$\frac{p\cdot u}{u\cdot u}u$. Plane $n\cdot x = n\cdot p$, distance of $q$:
$|n\cdot(q-p)|/|n|$. \textbf{Lines} $p + t\,r$, $q + s\,u$:
$t = \frac{(q-p)\times u}{r\times u}$, $s = \frac{(q-p)\times r}{r\times u}$;
parallel iff $r \times u = 0$; segments meet iff $0 \le t, s \le 1$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Matrices.} 2$\times$2 inverse $= \frac{1}{ad-bc}(d, -b; -c, a)$. Cramer:
$x_i = \det A_i / \det A$ ($A_i$: column $i$ replaced by $b$). $\det(AB) = \det A\det
B$; a row swap flips the sign. $Ax = b$ is solvable iff $\mathrm{rank}\,A =
\mathrm{rank}[A|b]$, then $p^{n-\mathrm{rank}}$ solutions mod $p$. Order-$k$ linear
recurrence: $k\times k$ matrix power, $O(k^3\log n)$; walks of length $L$:
$\text{adj}^L$.\\[0.3ex]
\textbf{Counting.} $\sum_k\binom nk = 2^n$, $\sum_k k\binom nk = n2^{n-1}$,
$\sum_k\binom nk^2 = \binom{2n}{n}$. Circle arrangements $(n-1)!$; $k$ from $n$ kinds
with repetition $\binom{n+k-1}{k}$. Fibonacci: $F_{2n} = F_n(2F_{n+1}-F_n)$,
$F_{2n+1} = F_n^2 + F_{n+1}^2$, $\gcd(F_m,F_n) = F_{\gcd(m,n)}$.}

\entry{Technique by symptom}{}{%
\begin{ctab}{0.43}{0.52}
\textbf{You see} & \textbf{Try}\\
answer is ``smallest $x$ such that \dots works'' & binary search on $x$\\
min of a max / max of a min & binary search, or sort + DSU\\
queries offline, any order & sort queries; DFS + rollback; Mo ($\sqrt n$ blocks)\\
``for every pair'' and $n \le 10^5$ & sort, two pointers, sweep, FFT\\
sum over all subarrays & contribution of each element\\
subsets and $n \le 20$ & bitmask DP, SOS\\
$n \le 40$ & meet in the middle\\
shortest path, few weights & 0-1 BFS (deque), Dijkstra\\
``number of ways'' mod $p$ & DP, combinatorics, matrix power\\
$k$ up to $10^{18}$ steps & matrix power, cycle finding, doubling\\
grid, ``each cell one of two'' & bipartite / flow / 2-SAT\\
intervals & sort by end (greedy), sweep with events\\
tree, all paths & centroid decomposition, rerooting\\
tree, path queries & HLD, LCA + prefix sums\\
DAG / game & DP in topological order, Grundy\\
strings, many patterns & Aho-Corasick, suffix array, hashing\\
XOR of subsets & XOR basis, trie\\
points, ``nearest / enclosing'' & hull, closest pair, min cover circle\\
exact formula unknown & brute force small cases, find the pattern\\
\end{ctab}}

\entry{When stuck}{}{%
Re-read the statement and the constraints. The bound on $n$ usually names the intended
complexity outright --- check the table above before designing anything.\\[0.3ex]
Write the brute force first, then stress test against it. A wrong answer on $n=3$ is
worth more than an hour of staring.\\[0.3ex]
Reframe: is it a graph? a flow? a matching? Can you binary-search the answer? Sort the
input? Process queries offline, sorted? Think backwards from the end? Count the
complement? Fix one variable and see what is left?\\[0.3ex]
Check the samples \emph{by hand}. If the sample passes but the judge does not, the bug is
almost always an edge case from the Pitfalls list --- most often multiple test cases, or
an overflow.\\[0.3ex]
